posts.author: Hans
posts.content_md:
When I expose MBDCG a short time, it will re-play in a golden broad band.

When I expose a longer time, it will re-play in a green colour.

The problem now is that the laser beam is so much brighter in the centre than in the sides that when I expose larger MBDCG plates, the middle of the plate always re-plays back in green and the edges in a golden broad-band. The changeover area is quite small and abrupt. Small plates are not a problem because I can then use the center part of the beam and massively expose the small plate enterely.

Does anyone know a remedy to this problem?

posts.author: JohnFP
posts.content_md: Have you tried to expand the beam to a larger diameter and then increase exposure time to make up for less energy?

posts.author: Hans
posts.content_md:
I have been tinkering with that thought, but the problem there is that I am already exposing 45 minutes with the current setup. Because I made the heat sink to my TEC controller too small, it overheats if I use it longer than one hour. I will try to make thinner coatings this afternoon. I hope that the thinner coating will allow more light to pass through the MBDCG and thus increase the beam ratio for higher sensitivity.

p.s. Does normal DCG have the same abrupt colour change on re-play with different exposure energies?

posts.author: JohnFP
posts.content_md:
There is a change in color with exposure energy with regular DCG, but I have never noticed it on a single hologram. I usually expand my beam a few inches larger then the plate.

Let me raise another point. If you are getting gold on the outer edge and that has much less energy, then why not calculate the amount of energy for the ouside edge, then expand your beam a little more, then expose accordingly. With a gaussian profile it would not be too far fetched if your outter edge is getting 1/2 the energy that you can expand without raising exposure time. Unless of couse you are trying to get green. I like gold better for final dispays.

posts.author: Hans
posts.content_md:
I will give that a try this evening. I like the gold also much better. 

The coating machine I have made works like a charm by the way. I will post info about it on the wiki if I can find the time this evening. Kris is also building one that will be much more professional than mine (I built it in one afternoon). Perfect coating each time all the way up to the edges.

posts.author: JohnFP
posts.content_md:
Show me yours and I'll show you mine.... Hehehe!!!

Actually, I am having great sucess with the bar rod. I take six 5x7 plates and lay them down in an array of 2 across (short edge) and three down (long edge). I then lay two more 5x7 plates long ways across the top. These two top plates are for where I pour the puddle and because they are laying long ways, they stick out past the edge of the 6 good lower plates. I then tape all joints and edges with a very thin tape. I heat the glass, pour the puddle, pull the bar and let set for two hours. I then untape and put the plates in a holding rack.

posts.author: Joe Farina
posts.content_md:
> **Hans:** I am already exposing 45 minutes with the current setup.

That's a pretty impressive exposure time, even remarkable if you are using a diode laser. Well done.

One minor drawback to MBDCG is (as you mentioned) that a lot of light tends to be absorbed by the MB, especially in thicker layers. In non-dye sensitized DCG, very thin layers are fine (say 5 microns) and are very good for bright, golden, broadband (but shallow in replay) holograms, just like the kind August Muth produces.

But I think the situation is quite a bit different in MBDCG, and I get the impression that thicker layers are best (based on the many papers I've read). Say for example in the 20 to 30 micron range. (A side benefit to thicker layers, according to Rallison, is that they are also the easiest to process uniformly, in contrast to thin layers.) So, I wouldn't suggest trying to increase transmitted light in MBDCG by making a thinner layer (I assume you're making unassisted, single beam Denisyuk holograms).

If you need better uniformity in terms of exposure across the plate, I would spread the beam out more, as John suggested. Of course a lot of light will be lost that way, but I would favor split-beam holograms in contrast to unassisted Denisyuk ones. Then the object beam could be increased as much as needed. This is where fringe-locking could be really helpful. Given your considerable skill in electronics, Hans, why not build a fringe-locker and see for yourself? In terms of project difficulty, on a scale of 1 to 100, I would say it's about 7.
